title: SLIs, SLOs & SLAs
summary: The measurement hierarchy that turns "reliable" from a feeling into a number you can page on and negotiate against.

slides.markdown:
Three letters, one chain: **SLI** is what you measure, **SLO** is the internal target you hold yourself to, **SLA** is the external promise with consequences if you miss it.

- SLI → SLO → SLA, each one looser than the last.
- The gaps between them are deliberate **safety margins**, not slack you forgot to remove.
- Get the SLI wrong and everything built on top of it — alerts, error budgets, contracts — measures the wrong thing.

slides.subTitle: The metric that represents user-perceived health
slides.markdown:
A **Service Level Indicator (SLI)** is a directly measured metric of your service's behavior — request latency, error rate, availability, throughput. It's a **quantity**, not a target: "99.95% of requests succeeded in the last 5 minutes" is an SLI value, not yet a goal.

The metric only matters if it reflects what a real user feels. A server's average CPU utilization is easy to measure but tells a user nothing; whether their checkout request succeeded does.

A good SLI is **user-facing, measurable, and meaningful**. Concretely: pick the ratio of "good events" to "valid events" — e.g. `HTTP requests under 300ms / total HTTP requests`, not a raw count that says nothing about proportion.

Common SLI shapes: **availability** (successful requests / total requests), **latency** (fraction of requests under a threshold), **freshness** (data updated within X minutes), **correctness** (output matches expected). Pick the smallest set that actually captures what breaks user trust.

slides.subTitle: The internal target built on an SLI
slides.markdown:
A **Service Level Objective (SLO)** is the target value you hold an SLI to over a window: "99.9% of requests succeed, measured over a rolling 30 days." It's internal — engineering and product use it to decide when to slow down and fix reliability versus ship features.

The SLO is where **error budgets** come from: 100% minus the SLO is exactly how much unreliability you're allowed to spend before you must prioritize reliability work over new launches.

slides.subTitle: The external, contractual promise
slides.markdown:
| | SLO | SLA |
|---|---|---|
| Audience | Internal (eng, product) | External (customers, contracts) |
| Consequence of miss | Feature freeze, reliability work prioritized | Credits, refunds, penalties |
| Typical looseness | Tighter — e.g. 99.9% | Looser — e.g. 99.5% |
| Who sets it | Engineering, based on what's achievable | Sales/legal, based on what's sellable |

The SLA is deliberately **looser** than the SLO so you breach your own internal target — and can act on it — well before you're on the hook for a customer payout.

slides.subTitle: SLI feeds SLO feeds SLA
slides.markdown:
![SLI feeds SLO feeds SLA, with safety margins between them](assets/sli-slo-sla-chain.svg)

Each layer sits looser than the one before it. That gap is what gives you room to notice and fix problems internally (SLO breach) long before they become customer-facing contractual failures (SLA breach).

slides.subTitle: Defining an SLI/SLO for a checkout API
slides.markdown:
For a checkout API, the SLI is `(requests completed successfully in < 500ms) / (total valid requests)`, measured per minute. The SLO: **99.9% over a rolling 28-day window** — chosen because past incident data shows the service already runs near 99.95% normally, leaving a real but not-impossible margin.

The SLA offered to enterprise customers: **99.5%**, with service credits below that — deliberately looser than the 99.9% SLO, so engineering has room to act before any contract is at risk.

slides.subTitle: The 100% SLO trap
slides.markdown:
Setting an SLO of **100%** feels safest but is actually self-defeating: it's physically unachievable (networks drop packets, disks fail, deploys have blips), and it leaves **zero error budget** — meaning any imperfection, however tiny, technically blocks every future launch.

The correct model: pick an SLO slightly below what you can realistically sustain, so there's a real, spendable budget for the inevitable rough day, without pretending failure never happens.

slides.subTitle: Load-balancer SLIs vs what users actually feel
slides.markdown:
An SLI measured at the load balancer only sees requests that actually made it there — it misses DNS resolution failures, client-side timeouts before the request ever left the device, CDN edge errors, and mobile-network flakiness, none of which reach your infrastructure at all. A service reporting 99.98% availability at the LB can still have real users experiencing meaningfully worse reliability than that number suggests, because the failures are happening upstream of where you're measuring.

The fix is measuring from more than one vantage point: **synthetic monitoring** (scripted requests fired from external locations that mimic a real client's path) and **real user monitoring (RUM)**, which captures actual client-side telemetry from real sessions. Treat a persistent gap between the LB-measured SLI and the RUM-measured one as a signal pointing at the network or edge layer — not as proof the service itself is unhealthy.
